title: Permission to Speak Freely
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 20 of 40
content:
Danse kissed me by accident.

Not literally.

Paladin Danse did very little literally by accident.

But the first kiss happened because neither of us had apparently planned beyond standing too close in a corridor.

The evening began with a debriefing.

We had spent the day clearing a raider position from an old research facility. Nothing unusual. Nobody seriously injured. Valuable technical documents recovered. By Brotherhood standards, an excellent mission.

Danse dismissed the squad and asked me to stay.

I stayed.

He closed the briefing-room door.

That was new.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You closed the door.”

“I’m aware.”

“You’re standing like you’re about to court-martial me.”

“I’m not.”

“Are you sure?”

His jaw tightened.

“Can I finish?”

“You haven’t started.”

Danse closed his eyes.

I smiled despite myself.

When he opened them again, the command was gone.

Nerves remained.

“I wanted to discuss what happened during the storm.”

“We slept.”

“Yes.”

“Scandalous.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

“I know.”

He paced once.

“I don’t want you to think I took advantage of the situation.”

I stared at him.

“You held me while we slept.”

“Yes.”

“I was there.”

“I’m aware.”

“I could have moved.”

“I know.”

“Danse.”

He stopped.

“You didn’t take advantage of anything.”

His shoulders eased.

“Good.”

“But that’s not actually what you’re worried about.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You do this too often.”

“Do what?”

“Make me say the part I’m trying not to say.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you’ll build a bunker around it otherwise.”

“That’s not fair.”

“Accurate, though.”

He looked away.

The room hummed with ventilation.

Finally he said, “Things are changing between us.”

“Yes.”

“I don’t know what to do with that.”

“You could try asking what I want.”

Danse looked genuinely startled.

“What do you want?”

There it was.

Simple question.

Terrifying answer.

I stepped closer.

“You.”

His breathing stopped.

Not forever. Just long enough to make me notice.

“That’s…”

“Yes?”

“Not an answer.”

“It is extremely an answer.”

“I meant specifically.”

I smiled.

“You want tactical detail?”

He realized how that sounded.

Color rose into his face.

“I mean—”

“I know.”

I rescued him because I was not cruel.

Usually.

“I want to spend time with you when we’re not working. I want you to stop pretending holding my hand is an administrative error. I want to see what this is without acting like wanting anything automatically makes it dangerous.”

Danse stared at me.

“I don’t know if I can give you that.”

The honesty hurt less than a false promise would have.

“Because of regulations?”

“Partly.”

“Cutler?”

His eyes flickered.

“Partly.”

“And the rest?”

He looked toward the Brotherhood emblem on the wall.

“I’m good at being a soldier.”

“I know.”

“I understand expectations. Orders. Objectives. This…”

His hand moved helplessly between us.

“I’m not good at this.”

I thought of him making terrible coffee for me. Tightening my vertibird harness. Writing maintenance notes. Sitting up all night with dead men’s lockers. Holding my hand through a radstorm.

“You are,” I said.

He frowned.

“You’re just not good at talking about it.”

That surprised a laugh from him.

“Maybe.”

“Definitely.”

I moved one step closer.

Danse did not retreat.

“Permission to speak freely?” I asked.

His mouth softened.

“Granted.”

“I think about kissing you.”

Every trace of military composure left his face.

I had never seen anything more charming.

“Oh.”

“That’s all you have?”

“I wasn’t prepared for that.”

“You asked for specifics.”

“I regret it.”

“No, you don’t.”

His eyes dropped to my mouth.

“No,” he admitted. “I don’t.”

The space between us became very small.

“Danse?”

“Yes?”

“Do you think about kissing me?”

His answer was barely audible.

“Yes.”

I waited.

So did he.

Then we both leaned in.

Our foreheads bumped.

I laughed.

Danse swore softly.

“Outstanding,” I whispered.

“Don’t.”

I was still smiling when he tried again.

The kiss was careful.

That was the first thing I noticed.

Not timid exactly. Controlled. Like he was afraid of assuming too much. His hand came up to my jaw and stopped there, warm against my skin.

I leaned closer.

Control became something softer.

His mouth moved against mine with a quiet hunger that seemed to surprise him as much as it did me.

When we separated, Danse kept his forehead against mine.

Neither of us spoke.

Then he said, “This complicates things.”

I laughed directly against his mouth.

“Of course that’s your first thought.”

“It’s true.”

“So is the fact that you kissed me.”

“You kissed me too.”

“Shared responsibility.”

“That sounds suspiciously like something I taught you.”

“See? Good officer.”

His thumb moved once along my cheek.

The gesture was so tender it hurt.

“I don’t know what happens next,” he said.

“Neither do I.”

He looked uneasy.

I added, “We don’t need a plan tonight.”

Danse stared at me like I had suggested abandoning gravity.

Then slowly, reluctantly, he smiled.

“One night.”

“One night.”

He kissed me again.

This time we did not bump foreheads.

The problem with kissing someone I had been circling for weeks was that afterward every ordinary interaction developed a second meaning.

Danse handed me ammunition.

My brain: *his hand was on my face last night.*

Danse asked whether I had checked the perimeter.

My brain: *his mouth was on mine.*

Danse leaned over my shoulder to inspect a map.

My brain stopped contributing useful information entirely.

“This route,” he said.

“What?”

His eyes narrowed.

“The northern route.”

“Right.”

“You weren’t listening.”

“I was distracted.”

“By what?”

I looked at him.

He understood.

His ears turned red.

“Oh.”

“Yeah.”

We both looked at the map.

It became the most interesting map in the Commonwealth.

Finally Danse cleared his throat.

“We should establish expectations.”

I turned slowly.

“Of course you want a briefing for this.”

“This is not a briefing.”

“Are there objectives?”

“No.”

“Rules of engagement?”

His expression became deeply pained.

“Please stop.”

I laughed.

The tension broke enough for him to breathe.

Danse sat on the edge of the desk.

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

He folded his hands.

“I don’t have much experience with…”

He gestured between us as though romance were a hazardous material.

“This.”

“I guessed.”

“That obvious?”

“You kissed me by walking into my face.”

His eyes closed.

“I had hoped we were never going to discuss that.”

“We will discuss it at our wedding.”

Danse’s eyes opened so quickly I nearly apologized.

I did apologize.

“Too much. Sorry.”

“No, I—”

He looked away.

“It surprised me.”

“Forget I said it.”

“I don’t want to.”

That silenced me.

Danse stared at his hands.

“I’m not promising anything I can’t give. I don’t know where this goes.”

“Neither do I.”

“But I would like to find out.”

The careful sincerity of it went straight through me.

I stepped between his knees.

“Okay.”

His hands settled at my waist and stopped there, giving me every opportunity to move.

I didn’t.

“What do you need?” he asked.

The question was pure Danse. Not *what are the rules*, not *what am I allowed to do*, but what would keep the person in front of him safe.

“Honesty.”

He nodded.

“No disappearing into duty every time something scares you.”

He frowned.

“That is very specific.”

“Experience.”

“I’ll try.”

“And you?”

Danse thought.

“Patience.”

“With you?”

“With me. With the Brotherhood. With the fact that I may not know how to balance both immediately.”

I rested my hands on his shoulders.

“I can do patience.”

His expression softened.

“Can you?”

“One more thing,” I said.

Danse’s expression became wary. “There’s more?”

“Public affection.”

He looked as if I had proposed treason.

“What about it?”

“I don’t need a performance. I also don’t want you acting like touching me is classified information.”

“That seems reasonable.”

“Say it without looking at the door.”

His gaze snapped back to mine.

“I wasn’t.”

“You were measuring escape distance.”

“I was assessing privacy.”

“Very romantic.”

He rubbed a hand over the back of his neck. “I’ve never done this.”

“I know.”

“I mean any of it. Not seriously.”

The admission softened me.

“Then we learn.”

“Together?”

“That is generally how relationships work.”

“I’m aware of the theory.”

I laughed.

Danse looked relieved to hear it.

“No.”

He laughed.

“But I can practice.”

“That will have to do.”

I kissed him.

This time he did not bump foreheads, freeze, or apologize.

He simply kissed me back, careful at first and then with growing confidence.

When we separated, he rested his forehead against mine.

“No wedding jokes for at least a week.”

“Three days.”

“Five.”

“Four.”

“Agreed.”

I smiled.

We did eventually leave the briefing room.

Danse opened the door, checked the corridor, then stopped.

I waited.

He looked at my hand.

Then, with the expression of someone testing a dangerous new piece of equipment, he took it.

Two scribes rounded the corner.

Danse almost released me.

Almost.

They saluted. He returned it with his free hand.

Neither commented.

By the time they passed, his grip had gone painfully tight.

“Still alive?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“Good first field trial.”

He exhaled something suspiciously like a laugh.

There it was: our first romantic negotiation.

Naturally, Danse had turned it into a treaty.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
